prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B048 alone, crediting Katori and Ye. It is the entry that best fits the test I apply most strictly. There is an original idea (trapping many neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels while the atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime), a demonstration by the people who proposed it, and independent reproduction in several laboratories and species, with consequences that were not available before, namely millimetre-scale redshift measurements, tighter tests of constants and a basis for redefining the second. It is a new tool that opens a door. The round-1 exchange has sharpened one thing for me. Eight of eight members converging on the same two names is not itself evidence, because several of us moved there from other first choices and all of us say we rely partly on memory for the chronology. What I rely on is the structure of the credit: Katori for the concept and the first realisation, Ye for taking it to record accuracy and for the many-body clock physics. Those are two different decisive contributions, and I do not see a third person whose claim is of the same kind.
statement.case_against: The objection I take most seriously is the one Johansson, Kroll and Lindroth each put in their own words: whether the lattice clock is a distinct invention or the next step in a precision-time lineage already recognised in 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks). My answer is that the lattice clock does not follow from either. It needs the magic-wavelength idea and gives a different regime, many neutral atoms probed at once, and the many-body (spin-exchange) effects that Kroll and Johansson cite are a physics result of their own. That answer holds only if the citation names the lattice clock and not clocks in general, so I have worded mine that way. The remaining weaknesses are not settled by argument. First, the chronology of the 2003 to 2005 papers has not been checked against primary sources by anyone here, including me. Second, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd, Hollberg and the Yb and Hg groups have real contributions, so a two-name credit is a judgement about who did the original work and not a complete account. Third, Higgs (B054) is still the purest original experiment on the list, and I am passing over it because of attribution, not merit.

responses.point: Lindroth says the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize control of single ions, whereas the lattice clock is many neutral atoms with the light shift cancelled, and that she would be more concerned if either Katori or Ye were dropped than about the split between them. She also relies on recalled chronology.
responses.response: I agree on distinctness and on not ranking the two names against each other. The chair's question about chronology is directed at the atomic-physics members, and I cannot answer it from primary papers; I am a microscopist and work from the record as it was presented to me. What I can say is what I would need to see. For my credit to stand, the magic-wavelength proposal and the first demonstration of a strontium lattice clock must come from Katori's group, and the record-accuracy and many-body results must come from Ye's group, before anyone else's. If you or Kroll can confirm that from the 2003 to 2005 papers and the later JILA results, I will hold the split. If an independent group demonstrated the lattice clock at the same time with an equally original contribution, I would want that said plainly, and I would not wave it away.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the many-body (spin-exchange) physics inside the clock makes it a physics result and not only a metrology advance, that the pending redefinition of the second should not be a reason to wait, and that waiting risks a missed or contested attribution as the field grows.
responses.response: I now give the many-body argument more weight than I did in round 1, because it answers the charge that this is the second discoverer doing it better. It is also an argument for Ye's name that does not depend on record numbers alone. On timing I hold my position: the verification is already in hand from several laboratories, and a metrological redefinition would follow from the work and not validate it. Your point about contested attribution growing over time is the one that persuades me most, since every year adds more claimants to a credit that is now close to unambiguous. I would ask you to keep the citation narrow, as you proposed, so that the ion clocks stay outside it. I have added the magic-wavelength mechanism to my own wording for that reason, and I prefer it to the more general phrase about a new regime of precision.

responses.point: Mehlig says the prior prizes sharpen the award only if the citation is worded around the magic-wavelength lattice and the resulting accuracy, and that the pending SI redefinition of the second remains an open timing question for him.
responses.response: I agree with the wording point and have changed my citation to follow it. On timing, I would ask you to say whether you hold the redefinition as a reason to wait or only as an open question. My own view is that tying a Nobel Prize to the schedule of a metrological body gets the logic backwards. The prize is for the discovery or invention once it is experimentally verified, and the 10^-18 results are already reproduced independently. I also note that you have moved away from KPZ because of the credit line, which is the same standard I apply to Higgs. I think the committee should apply it consistently, so I do not treat attribution as an excuse for one candidate and not for another.

responses.point: Johansson keeps circuit QED (B001) as a strong later candidate and says the pending redefinition should be used neither as a reason to wait nor to act. He also asks why the lattice clock is not simply the ion clock with better numbers.
responses.response: I agree that B001 is a strong later candidate, and your own recusal flag is the right instinct. The 2025 award is close enough that I would not put it forward this year, and Girvin and Huang are a real problem for a three-name credit. On ions versus lattices, the answer I would give is that an ion clock probes one ion, which limits stability, whereas the lattice clock probes many atoms at once with the light shift removed. That is a different design, not better numbers on the same one. That is why a lattice-clock citation should not mention ions, and why I do not think the 2012 prize forecloses this one. I also accept that you will not use the redefinition either way; for me it is not an argument for waiting, and I would not use it as an argument for acting either.

responses.point: Pearce raises the possibility of a second prize part and asks whether a credit set exists for any alternative that members who raised concerns would accept. He notes his own difficulty in judging the AMO chronology.
responses.response: I looked for a second part and cannot defend one. The constraint is three people across the whole configuration, and Katori and Ye already use two of them, so any second part would have one name, and none of the alternatives has a defensible single-name credit. B054 would need a principled rule for choosing among Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, and no member has supplied one; I do not think I can be absolutely sure who did the original work in collaborations of thousands. B019 has the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang problem that Eriksson and Mehlig raise. B025 needs five names. I therefore stay with a single part, and I keep B054 and B019 as the alternatives because, if the committee did reach a principled rule or a defensible slate, they are the two I would move forward first.

uncertainties: Whether the chronology of Katori's 2003 magic-wavelength proposal and first strontium lattice clock, against Ye's later record-accuracy and many-body results, holds up when checked against primary papers; no member has done so yet.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd, Hollberg or others have a claim strong enough to join or displace Katori and Ye; I cannot settle this from my own field.
Whether the full committee reads a precision-measurement invention as a physics discovery for the purposes of the prize, even with a narrow citation.
Whether a principled rule exists for naming three people from ATLAS and CMS; if one were agreed, B054 should be reconsidered ahead of my preferred configuration.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: I have been a Fellow of the University of Tokyo since 2025 and have long-running exchanges with the Tokyo-area microscopy community, and Katori is a Tokyo-based researcher. I have no known collaboration, joint publication or financial tie to Katori or Ye. I also share the Chalmers environment with Johansson, whose possible recusal on B001 does not touch the B048 configuration. I regard these as grounds for disclosure only, not recusal, and I will follow the chair's view if the committee decides otherwise.
